chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr and Ali ibn Hadid, from Jamil, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I have dirhams owed to me by a man, and he gives me wine in payment.' He said: 'Take it, then spoil it.' Ali said: 'And make it vinegar.'

244 - Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd, from Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Muhtadi, who said: 'I wrote to al-Rida (peace be upon him): 'I am your ransom, grape juice turns into wine, and vinegar is poured over it along with something that changes it until it becomes vinegar.' He said: 'There is no harm with it.'

245 As for what was narrated - al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Husayn al-Ahmasi, from Muhammad ibn Muslim and Abu Basir and Ali, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'He was asked about wine into which vinegar is put, and he said: 'No, except what comes from itself.'

This report does not contradict the reports we mentioned earlier, because it is understood as a type of recommendation, for it is recommended that the wine be left until it becomes vinegar by itself, and nothing that changes it, such as salt and other things, is thrown into it. And if it were done, it would not be forbidden, nor would the doer be sinful.

As for the report of Abu Basir which we mentioned earlier, from his saying 'There is no harm with it' when nothing is put in it that turns it, its meaning is: when something is put in it that dominates it, so it is presumed to be vinegar, and it is not like that, for example, a little wine onto which a lot of vinegar is thrown, for it becomes with the taste of vinegar. And with this, its use is not permissible until it is separated from that wine and made alone until it becomes vinegar.
So when it becomes vinegar, that vinegar becomes permissible at that time. As for before that, its use is not permissible in any state.

key_terms.إفسادها: Spoiling it (making it unfit for consumption)
key_terms.استحباب: Recommendation (a legal ruling indicating a preferred action)
key_terms.خَلّ: Vinegar (the product of wine's transformation, considered pure)
key_terms.خَمْر: Wine (naturally fermented grape juice, considered impure)
key_terms.طعم: Taste (used as a criterion for determining the nature of the substance)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on wine that has turned into vinegar in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes these narrations to distinguish between the physical transformation of wine into vinegar (istihlal) and the ritual purity (taharah) required for consumption. He clarifies that while adding vinegar or salt to alter the taste is permissible and does not render it haram, the preferred method (mustahabb) is natural fermentation to ensure complete conversion, a nuance critical for Shia jurists determining the validity of vinegar used in food or medicine.
